newsitem.title: DENMARK: INTERVIEW-Copenhagen Airport eyes cargo growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Copenhagen Airport eyes cargo growth.

text.p: Cargo operations are growing slowly at Copenhagen Airports A/S but the airport is looking to lure other cargo operators to the main Danish airport, Managing Director Niels Boserup said.
"We see a slow increase in our business with all cargo freighters," Boserup told Reuters in an interview.

Freight services operating from the airport on a regular basis are Singapore Airlines Ltd, Lufthansa Cargo AG and integrators DHL, TNT and UPS, Muk Air, Skypak, Maersk Air, Star Air, North Flying and China Airlines, an airport spokesman said.
Boserup said he was hopeful about luring other cargo operators to set up services at the airport in light of new German road restrictions.
Much air cargo bypasses Copenhagen airport and is moved in trucks to other European airports.
"Trucks are not allowed to operate on the German motorways during weekends now. It is becoming more difficult for the trucking operations to move freely."

"I think we will be able to convince some of the big cargo operators that it would be easier and cheaper for them to operate air cargo operations out of Copenhagen rather than trucking," Boserup said.
One factor blocking the airport from becoming a major hub was the fact that Scandinavian airline SAS operated only one all-cargo freighter, Boserup said.
"Our situation is affected by the fact that SAS, our flag carrier, is not an airline with all-cargo freighters," he said.
In 1995 Copenhagen airport handled 309,832 tonnes of freight and an increase of nine percent on this figure was expected for 1996, although data had not yet been published.
Boserup said Danish authorities had in the past prevented competition from entering the cargo market.

"For many, many years the Danish authorities protected SAS...so it was impossible for other cargo operators to operate in Copenhagen. The Danish airline Maersk wanted to establish a cargo service but they couldn't get permission," he said.
"If they had been able to operate 15 years ago then I'm sure we'd have a big operation today," Boserup said.
The airport is undergoing a 10-year expansion project totalling between six and seven billion Danish crowns.
One part of this project will be linking the airport to a railway station through which trains from Sweden will enter the European continent. The project is due to be completed in 1998.
"The Danish and Swedish authorities are considering having high-speed cargo trains. I think it's a fascinating idea to link the air cargo system and the railway system," Boserup said.
The problem with railway cargo was that handling had not increased in speed although trains travelled faster, he said.
"We're prepared to have a railway cargo station right at the airport," he said.
Boserup pointed out a success story for the airport when integrator DHL was planning to set up sub-hubs in Europe but eventually chose Copenhagen Airport.
The airport agreed to establish a cargo centre to help suit the needs of DHL, Boserup said.
Despite Danish wages being relatively high compared to other parts of the world, DHL has its lowest cost per unit from its Copenhagen operation, Boserup said.
"DHL has its cheapest operations in the whole of Europe here," he said.
